name: The Sundered Voussoir

detectability.signature: Twin gravitational shear lines converging on an invisible keystone point; subspace harmonics spike whenever the rift widens

proximity: Navigation instruments return three contradictory position fixes simultaneously
Starlight smears into vertical streaks near the shear lines
contact: Hull plating flexes along non-existent seams as local geometry shears
Crew report seeing the same corridor from opposing angles at once
prolonged_exposure: Gradual dimensional slippage leaves bulkheads out of phase with the ship
Unprotected crew members vanish piecewise into the adjacent dimension

phenomena: Visible distortion of starfield along the seam
Impossible geometries visible within the rift
Ships exiting at different locations than entered
known_incidents: The hauler Meridian Debt crossed a shear line in 2311 and exited nine light-years away, her crew unharmed but eleven days absent
A survey drone returned coated in mineral salts matching no known periodic table
description: To sensor telemetry the Sundered Voussoir presents as two vast planes of sheared spacetime grinding against one another, meeting at a single brilliant seam that hangs in deep space like the exposed edge of a broken arch. Visually, background stars stretch and splinter along that seam as though the sky itself were dressed stone under strain. The rift spans roughly twelve hundred kilometers and wanders slowly across the sector.

The rift dilates and contracts on no fixed schedule, though long-range monitoring suggests loose correlation with passing subspace pressure fronts. Vessels within a few hundred kilometers report tripled navigation returns and hull stress along impossible axes. Craft that touch the seam itself have been known to exit parsecs distant, or not to exit at all.

Charting followed the loss of the mining barge Kestrel's Tithe, whose distress beacon was heard from three directions at once. Subsequent survey established the rift's great age, placing its formation tens of millions of years before any known civilization. Cartographers now mark it as a hazard to be given a wide berth, though salvage interests persist.

Research buoys anchored at a cautious distance record continuous micro-shear events, feeding a scholarly dispute over whether the rift is widening geologically or merely breathing. Rumor holds that objects dropped through the seam sometimes come back altered. Pilots crossing the sector are advised to treat every second starfield reading as fiction.
